question.text: Mr. Ashwin Mehra, the GP of 'Yamuna Growth Fund III', is negotiating with an anchor LP (an insurance company) committing INR 250 crore out of a target INR 1,000 crore. The LP demands a 'management fee step-down' post the commitment period. From a manager's negotiation perspective, which of the following is the MOST appropriate structure?

answer.text: Refuse any step-down — management fee must be flat for the full fund life to cover operating costs
Step down fees to zero immediately after first close to attract more capital
Agree to step down from 2% on committed capital during commitment period to, say, 1.5% on invested (unrealised) capital post-commitment period, since deployment activity slows post-commitment period
Shift the fee to a pure performance-only model with no base fee at all

explanation.text: The Logic: Industry-standard practice (consistent with Section 13.3 and 13.4.1 negotiation points) is to negotiate a step-down: management fee applies on commitments during the commitment/investment period, then shifts to invested/unrealised capital at a lower rate post-commitment period. This aligns with reduced deployment work and is acceptable to LPs while preserving fund operating economics. The Trap: Flat fees are increasingly rejected by sophisticated LPs. Zero fee is commercially unviable. Pure performance-only model is rare and shifts risk entirely to manager. The step-down structure is the 'MOST appropriate'. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PMS) fee structures are simpler (fixed/performance). XIX-C manager must navigate the more complex LP-GP fee negotiation typical of private fund economics. Manager's Pro-Tip: Model the fee step-down in your PPM Illustration of Fees (Section XII) from Day 1 — LPs compare 'total fee load' over fund life, not the headline percentage. A clearly disclosed step-down can actually win commitments.
